answer:
Google's recommended architecture is a layered design with strictly unidirectional data flow.

- **UI layer** — Compose UI plus a ViewModel. Renders UI state, forwards user events. Owns no business logic.
- Domain layer (optional) — UseCase / Interactor classes that orchestrate a complex flow or combine several repositories. Skip it until a ViewModel starts doing real work.
- **Data layer** — one Repository per type of data, and it is the single source of truth for that data. The Repository hides its sources (RemoteDataSource over Retrofit, LocalDataSource over Room or DataStore) behind a domain-shaped API.

The rules that make it work: state flows down and events flow up; the screen exposes one `StateFlow<UiState>` collected with `collectAsStateWithLifecycle()`; the UI never mutates state, it calls the ViewModel; the ViewModel has no Android framework dependencies, so it unit-tests on the JVM; and data classes cross layer boundaries as domain models, not DTOs or entities.

The full guide is at developer.android.com/topic/architecture.

Clean Architecture is the same idea drawn as concentric circles and enforced harder: a pure-Kotlin `:domain` at the centre holding entities and use cases, adapters mapping DB rows and API payloads onto domain models, and Android, Retrofit and Room as replaceable outer frameworks.

The Dependency Rule is what both versions are really about: the domain never imports Android or Retrofit. The data layer implements interfaces the domain declares and DI supplies the implementation at runtime, so dependencies point inward even though data flows both ways. A pure-Kotlin domain module keeps its tests on the JVM and makes leaking a framework type into business logic a compile error.

When the stricter version pays: medium and larger apps, several teams, long-lived products. On a small app it is ceremony — Google's three layers are the same principle with far fewer classes.

A Repository is a single class that owns access to a domain entity, hiding WHERE the data comes from (network, DB, cache, in-memory).

### Why
- **Single source of truth** — UI talks to Repository, not directly to network.
- **Offline-first becomes natural** — Repository may serve from DB while refreshing from network.
- **Testable** — substitute a fake Repository to test ViewModels.
- Cross-cutting concerns (caching strategy, retry, mapping) live in one place, not duplicated across screens.

Best practice: Repository returns DOMAIN models (clean Kotlin types), never DTOs. Mappers convert wire/db rows ↔ domain at the boundary.

Unidirectional data flow means state travels down from the ViewModel and events travel back up from the UI.

- **State flows DOWN** — ViewModel → Composable / Fragment.
- **Events flow UP** — user actions → callbacks on the ViewModel.
- The UI never mutates state directly; it only asks for a change.

The resulting structure:

- `data class UiState(...)` — one immutable object that is the single source of truth for the screen.
- `StateFlow<UiState>` exposed by the ViewModel and collected with `collectAsStateWithLifecycle()`, so collection stops below STARTED.
- `fun onAction(action: UiAction)` (or individual methods) receives events.

Why it is worth the ceremony: there is exactly one place to look when the screen is wrong, the UI becomes a pure function of state so you can test it by handing it a state object, every action is loggable, and it matches Compose's rendering model — the same state always produces the same UI.

One-off events (navigate, show a snackbar) are the awkward case. Model them as a field in the state that the UI marks as consumed, or send them through a `Channel`; a `SharedFlow` with replay will re-fire them after a rotation.

A large app is normally split into one thin app module, one module per feature, and a set of shared core modules.

- `:app` — thin entry module that composes everything: nav graph, DI wiring, Application class.
- `:feature:*` — one per screen or flow: Compose UI, ViewModel, screen-specific state.
- `:core:domain` — pure Kotlin business types and use cases.
- `:core:data` — repository implementations, mappers, data sources.
- `:core:network` — Retrofit, interceptors, serialization config.
- `:core:database` — Room database and DAOs.
- `:core:designsystem` — colors, typography, shared composables.
- `:core:common` — small utilities (dates, formatting, dispatchers).

Dependency direction is the part interviewers actually probe: features depend on core modules and never on each other, `:app` is the only module that sees every feature, and cross-feature navigation goes through a route contract declared in a core module. A feature should compile against `:core:domain` interfaces, with `:app` binding the implementations.

What you gain: parallel compilation and far smaller incremental rebuilds, boundaries enforced by `internal` visibility instead of code review, per-module tests, and the ability to swap an implementation per build variant.

Share Gradle configuration through convention plugins in `build-logic` (a change in `buildSrc` invalidates the whole build cache), and declare versions once in a `libs.versions.toml` version catalog.

Android code becomes untestable when it reaches out for its dependencies instead of receiving them. Every pattern below follows from fixing that.

- **Constructor injection** — no static `getInstance()`, no framework singleton reached from business code.
- Wrap framework APIs behind interfaces — `Clock`, `Logger`, `LocaleProvider` — so a test can supply a deterministic version instead of the real clock or the real locale.
- Keep ViewModels free of Android imports: Kotlin types plus repository interfaces. Their tests then run on the JVM in milliseconds.
- Inject the dispatcher instead of hardcoding `Dispatchers.IO`, and use `kotlinx-coroutines-test` — `runTest`, `StandardTestDispatcher`, virtual time, `Dispatchers.setMain`.
- Prefer fakes over mocks for repositories: a fake keeps working as the interface evolves, while a mock encodes today's exact call sequence and breaks on every refactor.
- **Compose UI**: test a stateless content composable with `createComposeRule()` and a hand-built state object, addressing nodes by `onNodeWithText` / `onNodeWithTag`.
- **Instrumented tests**: `androidx.test.ext.junit` plus Hilt test rules; Robolectric when you want framework classes without a device.

Pitfalls: asserting on implementation details instead of observable behaviour, mocking types you do not own, driving everything through an Activity instead of testing ViewModel and UI separately, and tests that depend on real time or the real main dispatcher.

They differ in how the UI learns that something changed: a presenter calls methods on a view, a ViewModel exposes observable state, and MVI narrows that state to one immutable object changed only through declared actions.

- **MVP** — the view is an interface (`showLoading()`, `showItems(list)`) and the presenter holds a reference to it and calls those methods. State lives implicitly in the presenter's fields and in whatever the view happens to be displaying, attach and detach have to be driven by the lifecycle by hand, and two sources of truth are easy to end up with. Common in older View-based code.
- **MVVM** — the ViewModel exposes observable state and knows nothing about the view. The framework `ViewModel` surviving configuration changes is half the reason the pattern won on Android. Nothing forces the state to be a single object, so a screen with five separate flows that can disagree with each other is the usual failure mode.
- **MVI** — MVVM plus two rules: exactly one immutable state object per screen, and every change described by an action that a reducer applies. You get transitions that are trivial to unit-test, a loggable history of what happened, and no way to render an impossible combination. The cost is ceremony, and a naive implementation copies the whole state on every keystroke.

What a Compose app actually converges on is MVVM in name and MVI in shape: one `StateFlow<UiState>` of an immutable data class, a sealed `UiAction` handed to a single `onAction`, and updates through `_state.update { }`. Compose pushes you there because a composable is already a function of state.

Three follow-ups to be ready for. One-off effects such as navigation and snackbars are the case none of the three models well. MVI needs no library — a data class, a sealed interface and `update` are the whole pattern, with Orbit or Mobius as options rather than requirements. And the performance question is real: a large state copied per keystroke, or an unstable collection inside it, makes the whole screen recompose.

A UseCase is one business operation expressed as a single callable class, and it earns its place when the logic is shared between screens or too involved for a ViewModel to own.

The shape is deliberately boring: one public function, usually `operator fun invoke(...)` so the call site reads like the action, named in the product's language — `PlaceOrder`, `ObserveUnreadCount`, `SyncFavourites`. It takes repository interfaces in the constructor, returns domain models or a `Flow` of them, and imports nothing from Android, so it unit-tests on the JVM in milliseconds.

### What belongs in one
- Orchestration across more than one repository — folding a user, their subscription and their feature flags into a single answer.
- Business rules that belong to no single repository: whether the order can be placed, what the discount is, whether this content is allowed for this account.
- A transformation two or more ViewModels would otherwise duplicate.

### What does not
- A pass-through to one repository method. A class whose whole body is `repo.getUser(id)` costs a file, a DI binding and a test and buys nothing — call the repository from the ViewModel.
- **UI concerns**: formatting, string building, deciding whether a button is visible.
- Anything that needs a Context or a framework type.

Conventions interviewers check: the class is stateless, so it can be an unscoped binding; it receives a dispatcher rather than picking `Dispatchers.IO` itself; a Flow-returning one is named for observation and a suspending one for the action; and failures leave it as a domain result, never as an `HttpException`.

When the layer as a whole pays off: several ViewModels sharing rules, a genuinely complex domain, a team that wants business rules in one pure-Kotlin place. When it does not: a small app where every use case would be a one-liner. Google treats the domain layer as optional and says to introduce it once a ViewModel starts doing real work, and that is a defensible position to state.

A sealed hierarchy makes mutually exclusive phases impossible to confuse, while a single data class handles the far more common case where content, a refresh and an error are all true at the same time.

The sealed hierarchy wins when the phases genuinely exclude one another — a first load that shows a spinner and then either content or a full-screen error. The compiler forces the UI to handle every case with an exhaustive `when`, and there is no way to render a spinner over an error.

It breaks the moment the screen needs to do something while content is already on screen: pull-to-refresh, an error banner above a stale list, pagination appending to what is there. Expressed as a hierarchy, those all become a `Success` carrying `isRefreshing` and `error` fields, so you end up with both models at once. Worse, every transition throws the previous data away unless you copy it forward, which is why lists flash empty on refresh.

The single data class wins for a screen whose content stays put while things happen around it, which is most screens. `_state.update { it.copy(...) }` is a one-liner and nothing is dropped by accident. Its risk is impossible combinations the type system will not stop, such as `isLoading` and `error` both set. Keep the flags few, derive everything derivable rather than storing it, and never add a boolean that could be computed from the others.

The answer that lands well is to combine them: one data class for the screen, with a sealed type for the part that really has phases — a `content` field, or a per-section load state. Independent regions (the list, the filter bar, a dialog) get their own nested state objects so a change to one does not invalidate the other.

Practical rules for either shape: no Android types in the state class so it tests on the JVM; a `UiText` wrapper rather than a resolved string, so a locale change is picked up; immutable collection types so Compose can skip; and one `StateFlow` rather than five, because five flows mean five recompositions and a window where they disagree.

Combine the sources into the single state object the screen renders, then share the result with `stateIn` so a rotation does not restart every query underneath.

### The building blocks
- `combine(a, b, c) { ... }` produces the state from the latest value of each source. It emits nothing until every source has emitted at least once, so a source that may stay silent needs a default or an `onStart` emission — a screen stuck on its initial state is almost always this.
- `flatMapLatest` when one flow decides which other flow to observe, such as a selected id driving a details query. It cancels the previous inner flow, which is exactly what you want.
- `stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), initial)` turns the cold chain into hot shared state: one upstream collection regardless of how many collectors, kept alive briefly after the last one goes away.

That timeout is what interviewers push on. `WhileSubscribed` with a few seconds of grace keeps the upstream alive across a configuration change, because the UI resubscribes within a frame or two, yet stops the Room query or the socket when the user genuinely leaves. `Eagerly` starts immediately and never stops; `Lazily` starts with the first collector and never stops. Both keep working behind a backgrounded screen.

### The pitfalls that show experience
- The `combine` lambda re-runs on every emission from any source, so it must be a cheap pure projection. Suspending work goes upstream.
- An exception in any source cancels the whole combined flow permanently — a `StateFlow` that has failed never emits again. Wrap each source in `catch` and map the failure into a field of the state.
- `StateFlow` deduplicates by equality, so the state class needs correct `equals`; a data class over immutable fields has it, a mutable list inside one does not.
- Rebuilding one big object when any source changes is fine for Compose as long as the fields are stable, but an expensive section is better kept in its own state field so it can be skipped.

The alternative worth mentioning: collectors launched in `init` that each call `_state.update { }` on one `MutableStateFlow`. It is easier to debug and lets one section fail alone; `combine` is more declarative. Either is defensible — exposing five separate flows to the UI is not.

One-off effects misbehave because state is meant to be re-read while a command is meant to be consumed once, so anything replayed to a new collector runs a second time.

Who decides what: the ViewModel decides that the save succeeded and emits an outcome; the screen decides what that means for the back stack and calls the NavController. A ViewModel holding a NavController is the anti-pattern — it pulls a UI object into a class that outlives the composition, and it makes the ViewModel impossible to reuse or to unit-test.

### Why events double-fire
- A boolean in the state (`navigateBack = true`) is state, so it is read again after every configuration change and the effect repeats unless the UI acknowledges it and the ViewModel clears it.
- A `SharedFlow` with `replay = 1` replays to the collector that subscribes after a rotation. Same bug, different shape.
- `LaunchedEffect(Unit)` re-runs whenever the composable re-enters composition, which happens every time the user returns to a screen still on the back stack.
- Collecting without lifecycle awareness delivers events to a stopped screen, so the navigation happens underneath whatever is on top.

### What actually works
- A `Channel` exposed as `receiveAsFlow()` — each value goes to exactly one collector, is never replayed, and waits in the buffer if nothing is collecting yet. This is the default answer.
- `MutableSharedFlow(replay = 0, extraBufferCapacity = 1)` when dropping an event while nothing is collecting is acceptable.
- A state field plus an explicit acknowledgement callback — verbose, fully inspectable, and the only option that survives process death.
- Whichever you choose, consume it inside a `LaunchedEffect` that collects under `repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED)`.

For the snackbar specifically, Compose already gives you a better place: `SnackbarHostState.showSnackbar` suspends and returns the result, so "show it and undo if they tap Undo" is linear code inside the effect rather than two more events.

Two rules that keep this from spreading: use a typed `sealed interface UiEvent` rather than booleans, and never route ordinary state through the channel — anything that must still be true after a rotation is state, not an event.

Navigation arguments reach a ViewModel through its `SavedStateHandle`, which the framework fills in for you and which survives process death, so the common case needs no factory at all.

### How it works
- The ViewModel declares `SavedStateHandle` as a constructor parameter. With Hilt that is one more `@Inject` parameter on an `@HiltViewModel` class; with the default factory, `viewModel()` supplies it. Navigation puts every route argument into it.
- With type-safe routes, `savedStateHandle.toRoute<ProfileRoute>()` gives back the whole route object; with string routes it is `savedStateHandle.get<Long>("id")`.
- The same handle is where small state that must survive process death lives. `getStateFlow(key, default)` returns a `StateFlow` that is written back into the saved-state bundle — the ViewModel's equivalent of `rememberSaveable`, and bundle-sized: ids and flags, not lists of objects.
- The reason this beats writing a factory is that the argument survives process death for free and the ViewModel stays constructible by the framework.

When the value is not a navigation argument — something produced at runtime, or an object you would not want to serialise:
- **Assisted injection**: `@AssistedInject` on the constructor, `@Assisted` on the runtime parameter, an `@AssistedFactory` interface, and the factory handed to `viewModel(factory = ...)`. Hilt supports this shape directly.
- A hand-written `ViewModelProvider.Factory`, or the `viewModelFactory { initializer { ... } }` builder, for a small app.
- Best of all, avoid the problem: pass an id and let the ViewModel load the object from a repository, which keeps everything serialisable and process-death safe.

Anti-patterns worth naming out loud: an `init(id)` call after construction, which races the first state emission and silently breaks on recreation; passing whole objects as navigation arguments, which duplicates the source of truth and risks the Binder transaction limit; and reading the argument in the composable and pushing it into the ViewModel with a setter on every recomposition.

One scoping note: a ViewModel obtained inside a Navigation Compose destination is scoped to that back-stack entry, so one instance per screen is automatic, and scoping to the nav graph entry is how two screens in a flow share one.

Migrate screen by screen from the leaves inwards, adding a ViewModel first and Compose second, so that every commit is shippable.

The order that works:

1. Put the tooling in place with nothing user-visible: Kotlin and coroutines, a DI graph, the Compose compiler plugin with interop dependencies.
2. Move logic out of the Fragments into ViewModels while keeping the XML. This is where most of the value is — testable classes and state that survives rotation — and it is entirely independent of Compose.
3. Draw a data-layer boundary: a repository interface per data type with the existing code hidden behind it, so a screen can later be rewritten without touching networking.
4. Convert leaf UI first — a list row, an empty state, a dialog — hosted by a `ComposeView` inside the existing layout. Low risk, and it forces the design-system decision early, while it is still cheap.
5. Convert whole screens, still hosted by a Fragment, so navigation is untouched. `AndroidView` wraps the widget you cannot replace yet, such as a map or a video surface.
6. Only once most screens are Compose, replace the navigation layer and collapse toward a single Activity.

Interop details that actually bite: a `ComposeView` in a Fragment needs `setViewCompositionStrategy(DisposeOnViewLifecycleDestroyed)` or it outlives the view and leaks it; a Compose theme has to mirror the XML one so the two halves look identical during the transition; and a ViewModel shared between an XML parent and a Compose child works because both resolve to the same store owner.

What to resist: a big-bang rewrite branch that never merges; starting with the hardest screen to prove it can be done; and rewriting logic and UI in the same commit, which makes every regression ambiguous.

What keeps it honest: new screens are Compose-only by rule, a visible metric such as the share of screens migrated, characterization tests written around logic before you move it, and a per-screen flag for anything risky enough to need a rollback.

Where teams get stuck is worth naming: a design system that never quite gets built, so each screen reinvents its components, and the last twenty percent of screens that nobody owns. Saying that out loud is most of a good answer.
